author: reek
body: The pass condition is the guarded reader's: zero bad reads, and a real second recovered. What is NOT negotiable is that the guarded reader never once hands back a number that a clock cannot produce.

author: reek
body: The unguarded count is not printed at all, and that is a correction. It used to print `unguarded-bad-seen=y` or `n`, and the .expected pinned `y` -- which asserted it, whatever the paragraph above it said. The harness compares the whole output against .expected and has no channel for a line that is shown but not checked, so a varying line cannot be printed here at all. Measured over four runs on codex-vm it came back y, y, n, n: a coin flip sitting in the battery, failing half the release tallies for a reason that is not a defect. The probe still RUNS, because running it is what drags the clock across a tick and exercises the hazard for the guarded reader to survive; only its verdict is gone.

author: reek
body: The unguarded probe runs until the clock TICKS -- until a guarded read reports a different second than the one it started on. That spans a whole second boundary, and the update window lives inside every one of them.

author: reek
body: That was once written here as "so the hazard cannot be missed by getting lucky with timing". It can be missed, and the four runs above are the measurement. Spanning the window is not the same as catching a value out of range: a read taken mid-update returns whatever the chip has half written, and half-written is often still a number under sixty. Crossing the boundary makes the hazard LIKELY, not certain, which is why its verdict is no longer a pass condition.

author: reek
body: The unguarded reads must run in BURSTS. A guarded read waits the update out, so a guarded call between every unguarded one serialises the hazard away: the very next unguarded read lands just after the window and can never be caught by it. That is a trap worth stating, because a test that quietly prevents the failure it is looking for reports a clean bill of health for a broken system -- which is how this whole class of bug got as far as a hundred flashes.

author: reek
body: A guarded read that lands mid-update returns -1: "I could not read the clock", which is the honest answer and the one the caller is built to handle. It is not a bad value. A bad value is a number a clock cannot produce, and that is what this counts.
